claim: In METR's randomized controlled trial published July 2025, 16 experienced open-source developers working on 246 real issues from their own repositories took 19% longer when AI tools were allowed; before the study they forecast a 24% speedup, and afterwards they still believed AI had sped them up by 20%.

sources.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
sources.excerpt: when developers use AI tools, they take 19% longer to complete issues ... developers expected AI to speed them up by 24% ... they still believed AI had sped them up by 20%.

notes: Part of the mixed evidence base (see CLM-666). Randomization unit was the issue, not the developer. METR states it does not claim the developers or repositories represent most software work, and cannot rule out learning effects beyond 50 hours of tool use. METR has since marked these results as superseded by its February 2026 update (CLM-651). Design lessons used in the plan: randomize at task level where possible; do not rely on self-reported speedup.

claim: METR's February 2026 update, with data from 57 developers across 143 repositories and 800+ tasks using late-2025 tools, estimated speedups of 18% (confidence interval from 38% faster to 9% slower) for returning developers and 4% (15% faster to 9% slower) for newly recruited developers, but METR calls this an unreliable signal because developers increasingly declined to participate since they did not want to work without AI.

sources.title: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design
sources.excerpt: We have data from 57 developers, across 143 repos, and 800+ tasks ... we now estimate a speedup of -18% with a confidence interval between -38% and +9% ... developers choosing not to participate in the study because they do not wish to work without AI

notes: METR's sign convention: negative values mean tasks took less time with AI. METR concludes the new data 'gives us an unreliable signal of the current productivity effect of AI tools' and is redesigning its study. Design lesson used in the plan: participants who must work without a tool may decline or drop out (selection and attrition risk for comparison groups).

claim: A 2024 randomized controlled trial with 96 full-time Google software engineers estimated that AI features shortened time spent on an enterprise-grade task by about 21%, with a large confidence interval.
safeWording: A 2024 randomized trial with 96 Google engineers (published as a preprint) estimated about 21% less time on task with AI assistance, with a wide confidence interval; the authors caution that the effect may not apply more broadly.

sources.title: How much does AI impact development speed? An enterprise-based randomized controlled trial (arXiv:2410.12944)
sources.excerpt: We found that AI significantly shortened the time developers spent on task. Our best estimate of the size of this effect ... stands at about 21%, although our confidence interval is large.

notes: Partial because it is a preprint (no peer-reviewed venue listed on arXiv) using internal Google tooling in summer 2024. Part of the mixed evidence base (CLM-666).

claim: Google Cloud's DORA 2024 Accelerate State of DevOps Report found that AI adoption significantly increases individual productivity, flow and job satisfaction, but also negatively impacts software delivery stability and throughput.

notes: The web page states the direction of the effects without magnitudes; do not quote percentages from secondary sources. Part of the mixed evidence base (CLM-666). Design lesson: measure team delivery and stability guardrails, not only individual speed.

claim: As of October 2026, Claude Code applies managed settings above user, project and local settings. An organization can deliver them from the claude.ai admin console (server-managed settings), through MDM or OS policy (macOS configuration profile, Windows registry), or as a managed-settings.json file at /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/ (macOS), /etc/claude-code/ (Linux and WSL) or C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\ (Windows). A managed-settings.d/ directory lets several teams own parts of one file-based policy. Settings layers from highest to lowest are managed policy, the --settings flag, .claude/settings.local.json, the shared project file .claude/settings.json, then the user file ~/.claude/settings.json.

sources.title: Deploy managed settings

sources.title: Glossary
sources.excerpt: Settings layers: managed policy, settings you pass with the `--settings` flag, local settings at `.claude/settings.local.json`, project settings at `.claude/settings.json`, then user settings at `~/.claude/settings.json`.

notes: Drop-in directory: managed-settings.json is merged first, then every *.json in managed-settings.d/ in alphabetical order (numeric prefixes such as 10-telemetry.json, 20-security.json control order).

claim: As of October 2026, server-managed settings are fetched at startup and polled hourly, require a Claude for Teams or Enterprise plan and an Owner or Primary Owner role, apply uniformly to every user (per-group configuration is not yet supported), and are bypassed when a session is set up for a third-party provider such as CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK or CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX. MDM or OS policy is checked for changes every 30 minutes and a managed settings file is reloaded when it changes. /status (the Setting sources line) and claude doctor show which policy applied.

claim: As of October 2026, managed settings can lock down permissions and extensions: allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly and permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode make managed settings the only source of permission rules and disable --dangerously-skip-permissions; allowManagedHooksOnly restricts which hooks run; strictPluginOnlyCustomization limits skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers to plugins or managed settings; sandbox.enabled and sandbox.network.allowedDomains add OS-level isolation. Array settings such as permissions.allow and permissions.deny merge across sources, so developers can extend managed lists but not remove from them.

sources.title: Set up Claude Code for your organization
sources.excerpt: Array settings such as `permissions.allow` and `permissions.deny` merge entries from all sources, so developers can extend managed lists but not remove from them.

sources.title: Configure server-managed settings
sources.excerpt: "deny": ["Bash(curl *)", "Read(./.env)", "Read(./.env.*)", "Read(./secrets/**)"], "disableBypassPermissionsMode": "disable" ... "allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly": true

notes: The example deny rules Read(./.env) and Read(./secrets/**) are the documentation's own example policy. Permission rules and sandboxing cover different layers: denying WebFetch blocks the fetch tool, but with Bash allowed, curl can still reach any URL unless the sandbox network allowlist is on.

claim: As of October 2026, by default anyone running Claude Code can connect any MCP server they choose; Anthropic reviews connectors for its directory but does not security-audit or manage any MCP server. Administrators can deploy a fixed set with managed-mcp.json, provide remote servers to every user with managedMcpServers, or filter with allowedMcpServers, deniedMcpServers and allowManagedMcpServersOnly. managed-mcp.json cannot be delivered through server-managed settings, and credentials should not go in its env blocks because any user on the machine can read the file. Claude Code has no built-in registry that users can browse, so an approved list is shared on an internal page or distributed as plugins; claude mcp list shows which servers load.

sources.excerpt: By default, anyone running Claude Code can connect any MCP server they choose. ... Anthropic ... doesn't security-audit or manage any MCP server.

sources.title: Control MCP server access for your organization
sources.excerpt: Any user on the machine can read this file, so don't store API keys or other credentials in `env` blocks.

notes: The Security page covers the MCP threat model and how to evaluate a server before approving it. managed-mcp.json paths: /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-mcp.json (macOS), /etc/claude-code/managed-mcp.json (Linux and WSL), C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\managed-mcp.json (Windows). managedMcpServers requires Claude Code v2.1.259 or later and accepts https http or sse servers only.

claim: As of October 2026, MCP allowlist and denylist entries match servers by serverUrl (exact or with * wildcards), serverCommand (the exact command and arguments of a stdio server) or serverName. A serverName entry is not a security control because it is only the label a user assigns. A denylist match overrides everything. An unset allowedMcpServers allows all servers while an empty array allows none. With allowManagedMcpServersOnly set to true, user, project and local allowlists are ignored while denylists still merge from every scope. A blocked claude mcp add reports that the server is not allowed by enterprise policy.

sources.title: Control MCP server access for your organization
sources.excerpt: A `serverName` entry, in either list, is not a security control. The name is the label a user assigns when running `claude mcp add` or editing a config file, not the underlying server

sources.title: Control MCP server access for your organization
sources.excerpt: When `allowManagedMcpServersOnly` is `true`, allowlists from user, project, and local settings are ignored. The denylist still merges from every settings scope. | Nothing overrides a denylist match.

notes: User-visible message when an unlisted server is added: Cannot add MCP server "<name>": not allowed by enterprise policy. A server that silently disappears after a new restriction gives the user no signal that policy is the reason, so tell users what is blocked.

claim: As of October 2026, with OpenTelemetry export configured, setting OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 records MCP server and tool names in tool events and on the cost and token counters, and Claude Code logs a claude_code.mcp_server_connection event (status connected, failed or disconnected) when an MCP server connects, so administrators can see which MCP servers their users actually use. Without OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1, user-configured server names are replaced with "custom".

sources.title: Control MCP server access for your organization

claim: As of October 2026, managed settings can restrict which models and providers a machine may use and which versions may run: availableModels filters the model picker and, with enforceAvailableModels, also constrains the default model; allowedProviders limits the API providers (Claude Code v2.1.285 or later); minimumVersion stops auto-update installing below a floor and requiredMinimumVersion with requiredMaximumVersion refuse to start outside an approved range. On Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry the claude.ai organization model controls do not apply, so these managed settings are the route.

claim: As of October 2026, SSO, SCIM provisioning and seat assignment for Claude for Teams and Enterprise are configured at the Claude account level, not in Claude Code settings. On Amazon Bedrock, Claude Code uses the standard AWS credential chain, including an IAM Identity Center SSO profile (aws sso login with AWS_PROFILE), and awsAuthRefresh can re-run a command such as aws sso login when credentials expire. On Google Cloud's Agent Platform it uses standard Google Cloud authentication (Application Default Credentials, including Workload Identity Federation) and gcpAuthRefresh can re-run gcloud auth application-default login. A self-hosted Claude apps gateway can instead sign developers in with the corporate identity provider. Corporate VPNs or TLS-inspecting proxies can interrupt browser-based SSO flows.

claim: As of October 2026, Anthropic's champion kit sizes the champion role at about 15 minutes a week posting wins and prompts, about 20 minutes answering questions in a shared channel, about 5 minutes hosting a weekly show-and-tell thread, and 0 to 30 minutes of optional pairing (a single fifteen-minute session offered to anyone getting started). It recommends a dedicated channel, a Friday thread asking what Claude helped with this week, a four-week playbook (seed the channel, start the rhythm, pair and consolidate, hand off) with a signal of success for each week such as the same colleagues returning to use it, identifying the next champion, sending security and data-handling questions to the administrator, and /team-onboarding to generate a setup guide from a champion's own sessions.

The kit also warns that Claude Code ships frequently and version-specific details should be re-verified before internal distribution.

claim: As of October 2026, Anthropic's glossary defines agentic coding as a workflow where the AI can read files, run commands and make changes autonomously while you watch, redirect or step away, as opposed to chat-based assistants that only respond with text you must apply yourself. Claude Code works in a loop of gathering context, taking action and verifying results. Plan mode (entered with Shift+Tab or /plan) lets Claude research and propose changes without editing source files. Non-interactive mode (claude -p, formerly called headless mode) runs a single prompt and exits, for CI and scripts. A hook is a user-defined handler that runs automatically at a fixed point in Claude Code's lifecycle, deterministically rather than at the model's discretion. A subagent is a specialized assistant with its own context window, tools and permissions that returns a summary. MCP is an open standard for connecting AI tools to external data sources and services.

claim: As of October 2026, Anthropic's champion kit advises answering engineer concerns by acknowledging the concern, offering a brief reframe and proposing one concrete demonstration on the person's own code. Suggested replies: to "I am faster without it", try it on work you avoid such as legacy files, unfamiliar services or test scaffolding; to "I do not trust AI to touch production code", agree no change should land unread and use plan mode, then review the diff to the same standard as any pull request; to "it will make junior engineers weaker", ask Claude to explain a file and its call sites before changing anything; to "it hallucinated", supply context with @-mentions, /init and the real error output; to "no time to learn another tool", a two-minute install and one real bug.
